summary: Defines a BGP-4 optional parameter called Capabilities, which lets two peers advertise supported features without having to tear down the peering when new features come. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 3392.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2842 defines a way for BGP speakers to list optional capabilities in an OPEN message. A speaker can use a capability only after learning that its peer supports it.

questions: how do bgp peers negotiate features
what is bgp optional parameter type 2
what is bgp unsupported capability error
how do bgp peers advertise capabilities
subtitle: An OPEN-message parameter for advertising BGP features to a peer.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 required a speaker to end a peering session when it received an OPEN message with an unrecognized optional parameter, complicating the introduction of new capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The Capabilities optional parameter carries code, length, and value fields for each advertised capability. A speaker uses a capability only after determining that its peer supports it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2842 has been obsoleted by RFC 3392.

sections.title: Advertising Support for Capabilities
sections.content:
Before this extension, a BGP speaker had to terminate peering when an OPEN message contained an unrecognized optional parameter. That made it harder to introduce new BGP capabilities without disrupting a peering session.

A speaker that supports capability advertisement may include a Capabilities optional parameter in its OPEN message. It learns what its peer supports by examining the parameter in the OPEN message it receives.
sections.plainLanguage: Each BGP speaker can announce which optional capabilities it supports when opening a connection. It should use a capability only after seeing that the peer supports it too.

sections.title: The Capabilities Parameter
sections.content:
The Capabilities parameter is optional-parameter type 2. It contains one or more triples: a Capability Code of 1 octet, a Capability Length of 1 octet, and a variable-length Capability Value interpreted according to its code.

The same capability code may appear more than once in the parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: Each advertised capability has a code, a length, and a value. The code tells the receiver how to interpret that value.

sections.title: Handling Unsupported Capabilities
sections.content:
If a speaker receives an Unsupported Optional Parameter error in response to an OPEN message carrying Capabilities, it should try to establish the connection again without that parameter.

If a speaker supports a capability that its peer does not, it may send a NOTIFICATION with the Unsupported Capability error subcode, value 7. The notification lists the capability or capabilities at issue. Ending peering is a local decision, and the RFC says that peering should not be re-established automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: A peer that cannot handle the Capabilities parameter can be contacted again without it. A speaker can also end peering if a capability it needs is unsupported.

sections.title: Capability Code Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC expects IANA to maintain a registry of Capability Code values. Code 0 is reserved. Codes 1 through 63 use IETF Consensus, codes 64 through 127 use First Come First Served, and codes 128 through 255 are for Private Use.

The RFC says this extension does not change the security issues inherent in BGP.
sections.plainLanguage: The code space is divided into ranges with different assignment rules. The RFC says the extension does not change BGP's underlying security issues.

references.text: Rekhter, Y. and T. Li, "A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)", RFC 1771, March 1995.
